segments.text: The king of Qin has just swallowed the last of six rival kingdoms.
Six years earlier, this same man ran for his life around a pillar.
The assassin's dagger missed.
He survived.
Now he wants something no dagger could take: control over what history calls him after he dies.
And to get it, he must abolish a custom older than his dynasty.
When a Chinese king died, his sons and ministers gave him one last name.
A verdict.
"The Cultured." "The Martial."
Or, forever, "the Cruel."
And the dead could not argue.
He said: a son judging his father? A minister judging his lord? No.
No one would grade him. Instead, they would count.
He would be the First.
After him, the Second.
Then the Third.
All the way to ten thousand.
And yet, about his own beginning, history could not agree.
To see why, we go back to Handan, the capital of Zhao, Qin's old enemy.
Qin's armies were attacking Zhao again and again.
And inside Zhao's capital lived a prince of Qin.
Kingdoms in those days traded royal sons as hostages, a living promise of good behavior.
When the two kingdoms were friendly, a hostage lived well.
When they were at war, he lived badly.
And Qin and Zhao were nearly always at war.
Every time Qin's armies won a battle, the people of Handan looked at that prince a little harder.
His food got worse.
His guards got colder.
His own father's soldiers were the reason his life kept getting smaller.
This hostage prince would one day be the boy's father.
A rich merchant looked at this forgotten prince and saw an investment.
His name was Lü Buwei.
He spent his fortune making friends in Qin's court, working to get the prince named heir to the throne.
And there was a woman.
China's great ancient history tells it two ways.
In one chapter, the prince met her, liked her, and married her.
She gave birth to a son.
In another chapter, she had first been with the merchant, and was already pregnant when she was given to the prince.
Which is true?
People have argued for two thousand years.
There is not enough evidence to settle it.
What we know is this: the boy was born in Handan, in the capital of the enemy.
Later he went home to Qin.
At thirteen, he was king.
Years passed.
Qin's armies pushed east.
City after city fell.
Kingdom after kingdom.
Not even a dagger in the palace could stop them.
In 221 BC, the last kingdom, Qi, surrendered.
Six kingdoms. Gone.
Everything that had belonged to seven kings now belonged to one.
Which raised a question.
What should he be called?
There had been a king of Qin.
A king of Zhao.
A king of Chu.
Strong or weak, every one of them was called "king."
Now he stood above six fallen kings.
He was no longer one king among many.
"King" was too small.
He told his ministers to find something better.
The chancellor, the chief censor, and the chief justice, a man named Li Si, studied the old legends.
Long ago, the stories said, there had been a Heavenly Sovereign, an Earthly Sovereign, and a Supreme Sovereign.
The Supreme Sovereign was the highest.
That, they said, should be his title.
He read their proposal.
And he changed it.
He struck out "Supreme."
He kept "Sovereign."
Then he took a second word, Di — the title of the legendary god-kings of ancient times.
He joined the two.
Huangdi.
In English, we say it with one word.
Emperor.
Everything about how he spoke changed too.
His commands got a special name.
His decrees got another.
Even the word "I" changed.
There was an old word for "I" that anyone could use.
From now on, only the emperor could say it.
He honored his dead father as the father of an emperor.
And for himself: the First Emperor.
The rest, his heirs would count.
Second Emperor.
Third Emperor.
He hoped it would go on for ten thousand generations.
A new dynasty needed new colors.
People then believed that history turned on five forces: metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
Each dynasty ruled by one.
The old royal house had ruled by fire.
Qin claimed water.
Water puts out fire.
And the color of water was black.
Court robes turned black.
Banners turned black.
Six became the sacred number.
Ceremonial objects and carriages were measured in sixes.
Even the great Yellow River got a new name: the River of Virtue.
The river did not notice.
It flowed east as before.
Farmers still plowed beside it.
But in the capital, even the river belonged to the new order.
The title was settled.
The ceremonies were settled.
Now came the hard part: who would rule all the conquered land?
The court split.
The chancellor, Wang Wan, spoke first.
The lords of the old kingdoms have only just been crushed, he said.
Yan, Qi, and Chu are far away.
Without kings there, there is no one to hold them.
Send your sons, he asked.
Make them kings there.
Most of the ministers agreed.
Think about what "far away" meant then.
Every message, every army, had to cross that distance on foot, by cart, or on horseback.
That was how the old royal house had done it, centuries before.
One man did not agree.
Li Si.
The chief justice.
He said: the old royal house gave land to its own sons and brothers, too.
Over the generations, they drifted apart.
They attacked each other like enemies, and the king above them could not stop them.
We have only just ended that war, he said.
Do you want your grandsons to fight it all over again?
Now the land within the seas is one, thanks to Your Majesty.
Make it commanderies and counties.
Reward your sons and meritorious ministers generously — with tax revenue, not with kingdoms.
That is easy to control.
And no one will dare dream of rebellion.
Two plans lay before the emperor.
One: send his sons out to hold the land.
Two: send officials.
Men come and go.
The land stays with the throne.
He chose Li Si.
The world, he said, had suffered endless war because there were kings.
To set up kingdoms again would be to plant war with his own hand.
Then he said only this:
"The chief justice is right."
No new kings were made.
The empire was divided into thirty-six commanderies, each with a governor, a military commander, and an inspector.
Below them, counties.
An official could be sent anywhere.
Fired for a mistake.
And no governor could leave his commandery to his son.
The map was redrawn.
The choice could not be undone: there would be no princes out there to hold the land.
Only officials.
And officials can only obey what they can read, measure, and reach.
Picture a county town in the old land of Chu, newly under Qin.
The walls are the same old walls.
The market opens like it did last year.
Farmers go out to the fields.
The dynasty has changed, but people still have to eat.
What has changed is inside the county office.
An appointed stranger sits there now, and he answers to the capital.
He must count the households, measure the fields, weigh the grain, and send it all up — to the commandery, and from there, all the way to the emperor.
To do that, he needs three humble things.
A wooden slip he can read.
A measure he can trust.
A road his reports can travel.
Follow those three, and you see how the empire actually ran.
Start with the slip.
His first problem: his orders may not mean the same thing here.
The same word could be written differently in Qin and in Chu.
Copy a place name wrong, and an order goes to the wrong town.
So Qin's script became the standard.
Clerks wrote it fast, in a working hand you can still see on slips dug from the ground.
Handwriting still differed — but an order written in one county could be read in the next.
Then the measure.
This problem was harder, because it was about grain — and grain was tax.
One town sends ten measures.
Another scoops it with its own old basket.
Both write "ten."
The amounts don't match, and each blames the other.
So the emperor ordered one standard for volume, weight, and length.
Museums today hold bronze Qin weights with his decree carved into the metal.
Two thousand years later, you can still read the command.
Then the road.
Roads back then were mostly packed dirt.
Year after year, cart wheels cut deep ruts into them.
But every kingdom had built its carts a little differently.
A cart from one region, with its wheels set at one width, would bump along ruts carved by someone else's axles.
One wheel in the groove, one wheel riding the edge.
In the rain, it sank.
So Qin set one axle width for every cart.
Of course, a decree doesn't swap out every axle overnight.
Old carts kept rolling for years.
But every new cart was built to the same gauge, and slowly, the ruts began to match.
The year after unification, work began on great imperial highways running out from the capital — with bridges.
Officials traveled them.
So did armies.
And so did the files.
There was no paper.
Reports were written on strips of wood and bamboo, bundled, tied, and sealed with clay, so no one could open them on the way.
A courier carried the bundle to the next station.
There, someone logged it — what arrived, when, from whom — and sent it on to the next.
Station by station, a county's report crossed the empire.
Then the answer came back the same way.
At Liye, in the south, archaeologists pulled tens of thousands of these wooden slips out of an old well — the files of a single Qin county office.
Some record when a document arrived and who handled it.
And some show a clerk running out of patience.
A reply was missing.
So he wrote again — in effect: did my letter arrive?
Where is the reply?
A small official, chasing another small official, over some piece of business two thousand years old.
That is how a far-off county was tied to the throne.
Not by the emperor riding out to see it — by a clerk who would not let a letter go unanswered.
But a county that obeys on paper can still rise up — if it has weapons, and men to lead it.
So weapons rolled into the capital.
Swords. Spears. Halberds.
The arms of six fallen kingdoms.
They were melted down.
The metal became great bells, bell stands, and twelve giant bronze men set outside the palace.
The old history says each of those figures was enormously heavy — by its own ancient measure, many tons of bronze.
None survives.
But once, the weapons of six kingdoms stood there as men who would never move.
Then he moved the men who might lead.
The rich and powerful families of the old kingdoms.
Their kings were gone.
Their influence was not.
One hundred twenty thousand households were moved to the capital.
Households — not people.
Picture what that meant for one of them.
A house your family had lived in for generations.
Fields your grandfather had bought.
Streets where everyone knew your name and owed you a favor.
All of it, left behind.
Nobody asked them whether they wanted to go.
In the capital, they were just newcomers.
Their old friends, their old debts, their old hold over the countryside — none of it traveled with them.
They settled right under the emperor's eye.
And their wealth went to work for his city.
So look at the capital now.
Xianyang.
For more than a century, it had been the seat of a strong kingdom in the west.
Now it was the center of everything.
Reports poured in from every county.
Orders poured out.
Couriers on the roads, carts on the matching ruts, bronze weights in the granaries, one script on every slip.
In the palace stood the twelve bronze men.
Around the city lived the great families of six kingdoms, far from home.
Out in the old kingdoms, the names were still there.
Zhao was still called Zhao.
The old palaces still stood.
The old city walls still stood.
The rivers still ran past them.
They just didn't belong to six kings anymore.
The emperor could never visit every county town.
He didn't need to.
From Xianyang, he could know how many households lived in a valley he had never seen.
How much grain sat in a granary he would never walk into.
The map that once showed a strong kingdom in the west now stretched all the way to the sea.
But look at the map again.
Look north.
Past the last counties, the hills roll into grassland.
Horsemen there came and went, fast.
No county office reached them.
No measuring cup.
No wooden slip.
Long before, Qin, Zhao, and Yan had each built walls along their northern frontiers, on ridgelines, across mountain passes.
Now those kingdoms were gone.
The walls were still there — scattered, separate, some crumbling.
Guarding borders that no longer existed.
And beyond them, the horsemen were still riding.
Scattered walls, on the ridgelines of the north.
The Great Wall.
